title: The song of the reed
hookLine: the Masnavi opens with a reed flute crying for the reedbed it was cut from (Masnavi 1.1–18)

cards: There's a sound some people can't hear without their chest tightening. A cello. A train whistle at night.
A certain voice on an old recording. It isn't even sad on purpose, and yet it opens something.
In the Mevlevi ceremonies of Konya, the ones people call the whirling dervishes, the music often begins with one breathy, low, wavering flute, alone. It sounds like someone missing someone.
Rumi's great book begins with that sound, and its verse opens with one word: listen. Today's word is the flute: ney.

teach.h: A HOLLOW REED, HOLES BURNED IN.
teach.b: The ney is a simple thing: a hollow reed, cut from a reedbed, with holes burned into it. You blow across the top, and your breath becomes a voice.
It's been played across the Persian, Arab and Turkish worlds for centuries. And in the opening lines of the Masnavi, it talks.
In E. H. Whinfield's 1898 translation, the book begins: "Hearken to the reed-flute, how it complains."

Ever since it was cut from the reedbed, the reed says, its crying has made men and women weep. It wants a heart torn by parting, someone who knows what being cut off means, so it can tell them the pain of longing.
And its song, it says, is not wind. It's fire. One way readers hear it: the reed is the human soul, taken from where it began, near God, and set down in this world.
The crying is the longing to go back. And the music, the thing that makes people weep, only happens because of the cutting. No reedbed, no flute.
No separation, no song. Some read the reed as Rumi himself, the man who lost Shams and found his voice. Some hear the saint or teacher, emptied so that another's breath can play through.
The poem lets all three stand.
Rumi begins his life's great book not with an argument but with a sound: something cut from the reedbed, and singing because of it.

how: In the Mevlevi sema ceremony, the ney plays a central part, often opening with a solo improvisation, and the first eighteen couplets of the Masnavi, the song of the reed, are often recited and taught on their own.

in the poem, the reed's song comes from its separation

there's only one right way to read the reed

games.q: you're a reed, cut from your reedbed and burned with holes. what do you do?
o: stay silent and wait to rot.
cry out, and let your crying become music.
games.why: the reed cries, and its crying makes men and women weep. its song exists because of the cut.

practice: Play one sad song you love, or, if you can find one, a recording of a ney, and do nothing else: don't sing along, don't scroll. Notice where it lands in your body and what it makes you miss.
You don't have to name it; let the song say it for you, the way the reed does.
